A lowland species found mainly below 200 m elevation, which is certainly true of known Australian populations, but it has been recorded from 0--1500 m elevation across its range. Typically found on sandy to clay soils along watercourses, along the margins of swamps and in seasonally wet savannahs in fully exposed to moderately shaded situations. It typically favours drier situations than N. rowaniae and N. tenax where the species co-occur, whereas in various parts of Southeast Asia it has been documented growing in permanent bodies of shallow water. High elevation populations are more typically observed in large mountain complexes or upland plateaus as a result of the Massenerhebung (mountain mass) effect, which sees warmer conditions manifested at higher elevations (A. Robinson, pers. obs).

Prior to 2005, all recent revisions of Nepenthes maintained Danser’s (1928) broad interpretation of N. mirabilis in Australia, however, these revisions were undertaken with no documented study of materials held at Australia’s major herbaria, in particularly BRI, or indeed of plants growing in situ to formally document any ecological differences between the proposed taxa (Clarke & Kruger 2005), as well as the degree of reproductive isolation that they might exhibit. Occurs as a component of coastal vegetation from Carnarvon to Perth in Western Australia and from E of Albany in Western Australia to Portland in Victoria; also in inland South Australia, western Victoria and western New South Wales. There are isolated records from the Northern Territory and Queensland, which may represent introductions through agricultural activities.

Clearance of Nitraria billardierei for control of feral species is often a controversial subject. It has been allowed in some parts of South Australia under State legislation but permission still needs to be sought from the Native Vegetation Council. Leaves and inflorescences often have gall-like infestations and these may well prove of interest since gall-forming armoured scale insects (Diaspidiotus species) have been documented on Nitraria species elsewhere (E.M. Danzig, J. Zoosyst. Rossica 8: 287--289 (1999). Similarly, the sphecid wasps Solierella nitraria Pulawski and Cerceris nitrariae Morice (R.M. Bohart & A.S. Menke, Sphecid wasps of the world: a generic revision (1976)) described from Egypt and Morocco respectively, were named for their association with Nitraria species and it would be interesting to see whether these same associations occur in Australian populations. The fruits of Nitraria billardierei are edible and particularly attractive to emus, and possibly to rock-parrots (S.A. White, Emu 16: 1--15 (1916)), but are also taken by kangaroos, sheep, rabbits, lizards and decorator ants; germination was found to be enhanced after passage through an emu (J.C. Noble, J. Ecol. 63: 979--984 (1975)). N. billardierei fruits have also been recorded as part of the diet of Australian Aborigines (B. Gott, Telopea 12: 215--226 (2008)) and have been eaten without any ill effects by the author. They have potential for development as a native food, although a little salty. Possibly not distinct from the Russian species Nitraria schoberi. While there is a documented chromosome number difference (2n = 24 for N. schoberi and 2n = 48 for N. billardierei), morphological differences, including spininess and leaf and floral characteristics, have not been investigated fully. Morphological differences, including habit and size of the stones, were documented by Noble & Whalley (1978a) between the populations of Nitraria billardierei occurring along the Indian Ocean and those which occur along the Southern Ocean. Again, a molecular study across the range of the species could prove useful, particularly given the expanding distribution in inland areas.

There is conflicting information on this species. The seeds are reported to be mucilaginous on wetting but those which were observed showed no evidence of any mucilaginous substances. Instead, the outer reticulately-marked surface expanded, apparently trapping a great deal of air between it and the embryo. Seeds also yield a dye called “Turkey Red” used for colouring tarbooshes (Mabberley 1987: 437) and for dyeing carpets in Turkey and Iran (Emboden 1972) but other references within dyeing books also attribute the dye known by this name to Madder (Rubia tinctorum). The colour of the dye extracted from the seeds depends on whether the extraction is done in water (yellow fluorescent) or alcohol (red). Peganum harmala plants have an unpleasant smell and are possibly poisonous to livestock. The alkaloids contained within the roots and seeds possibly account for this, as they may also account for a number of reputed medicinal properties ranging from emetic to antispasmodic, narcotic, stimulant and antihelminthic (Ghafoor 1977: 9). Emboden (1972) also refers to the aphrodisiac, narcotic and hallucinogenic properties of Peganum harmala. The properties of Peganum harmala are also provided by Parsons & Cuthbertson (2001: 637--639).

Mr William Archer (pers. comm.), who has made a study of this species, found that over 90% of a population reappeared each year even though they may have had their fronds eaten by animals or collected in the previous season. Within populations, the size of the plants can vary considerably and extremely small plants may produce a frond a few centimetres long. In such small plants the fertile sporophore is simple, with the sporangia in 2 rows; however, there are usually paired sporangia at the base of the sporophore. The pinnae are also variable within populations. Thus, although they usually have entire or slightly irregular margins, these are occasionally prominently crenulate and often have 1 medial or a number of incisions dissecting the pinnae. This latter situation appears to correlate with very robust plants. Very rarely up to 3 fertile sporophores may arise on a frond, each with its own stipe. I have also observed the occasional plant of B. australe to produce a second fertile sporophore.

Flowers exposed to the sun are pollinated by a small stingless bee, Tetragonula carbonaria, which, with extended mouthparts, forces its way to base of labellum (Jones 1981). The bee probes the calli and labellum sac for about 30 seconds before backing out, often receiving the orchid’s pollinarium on the thorax. After emergence from the flower, the insect cleans its antennae, mouthparts and front legs assiduously as if collecting an important compound. The fragrant flowers last less than day, opening early in morning and often finishing by midday. Sections of flowers on the racemes open simultaneously in spasms and generally all the plants in an area flower at same time, known as synchronous flowering or massed gregarious flowering. The whole area becomes saturated with a spicy perfume which stimulates local insects and allows the orchids to compete successfully for their attention. Tetragonula carbonaria also pollinates Pomatocalpa macphersonii, this time picking up the orchid pollinarium on the head. Flowers in the shade are uncommonly pollinated.

The flowers open fully during day and partially close at night with the tepals incurving over the column and labellum. The flowers last 1--3 days and have a fruity fragrance that specifically attracts male fruit flies of the genus Bactrocera (order Diptera, family Tephrotidae); 2 common native species are B. jarvisi and B. tryoni. These male fruit flies do not attempt to mate with the flowers but instead feed in the flower and take in chemical components of the floral fragrance which are vital for specific aspects of the insect’s sex life and reproduction (Tan & Nishida 2007). The flies visit the flowers in the morning and probe the sepals and petals, eventually feeding on the labellum which tips when the point of balance is passed trapping the insect against the column. While attempting to retreat the fly becomes stuck firmly in the viscidium, sometimes for more than 30 minutes, all the while struggling until eventually it frees itself with the pollinarium attached to its back. Pollination occurs when the insect visits another flower. See also Teck et al. (2011). Sometimes the insect perishes after becoming trapped in the flower (Smythe 1969, personal observations).

Plants produce inflorescences over 4--6 weeks during the wet season. All the flowers on an inflorescence mature and open together. They release a light, fruity perfume in periods of warm, humid weather. Nectar is produced in large droplets and coalesces in the base of the labellum. A pollination study in Atherton, Qld, using cultivated plants of this species, originally obtained from the McIlwraith Range on Cape York Peninsula, showed that the fly Silba excelsa (order Diptera, family Lonchaeidae) was attracted to the flowers to feed on nectar (Jones & Gray 1975). The flies feed on nectar on the labellum, moving into the flower until the labellum tilts, trapping the fly between the labellum and the stelidia on the column. The fly struggles and backs out of the flower, picking up the pollinarium on its thorax. Pollen is transferred to the stigma of another flower on a subsequent visit.

Australian populations of this orchid have been decimated by over-collecting. The relatively large flowers release a strong, unusual scent that smells like semen or fish meal. Nectar, exuded in large droplets, coalesces in the labellum groove and also flows into small pouches formed by the lateral sepals. The scent is very noticeable on warm days and attracts blowflies of genus Calliphora (family Calliphoridae), particularly C. tibialis, which actively work the flowers and feed on the nectar. The labellum tip is at first outwards as the fly feeds, but as the fly moves forwards the labellum eventually tips inwards and traps fly between the column and labellum. The fly buzzes furiously while trapped, eventually picking up pollinarium on its thorax. Pollen is transferred to the broad, sticky stigma of another flower on a subsequent visit. For details of pollination see Jones (1985).

The type specimens were collected in September-October 1921 by Edward Edgar Pescott, presumably with the assistance or direction of Bertha Pilloud. The orchid was reported at the time to be locally common, however numbers declined significantly as land was cleared for agriculture. The last reliable record was made in 1926 and the species was not seen again for 83 years, despite many searches, until an opportunistic discovery of two flowering plants in 2009 by orchid enthusiasts Hans and Christa Korth. The species is now the subject of a rigorous conservation program.

The flowers have a sweet, musky scent and attract male short-tongue bees, Leioproctus obscurus (family Colletidae), apparently by sexual deceit (see Kuiter 2014). Normally these bees feed on nectar in native legumes, but Caladenia rosella is nectarless. Only male bees have been seen on the orchid flowers and they approach downwind as if following a scent trail. Pseudocopulatory movements have been observed when the bees are on the labellum. Male bees emerge earlier than female bees in their life cycle and the flowering time of the orchid may exploit this numerical disparity of the sexes. Details on ecology also provided by Carr (1988: 445).

It is also often seen flowering in mowed or slashed areas. Usually only 1 or 2 flowers are open at any time. The flowers are sturdy and quite long-lived, lasting for several weeks if not pollinated or burnt by bushfires. In dry seasons the leaves are often withered by the time flowering takes place. The final flowers of the season, which open towards the end of spring, survive well into summer if conditions are amenable. Flowers have even been recorded as late as May, a six-month flowering period (Jones 1970). Remarkably these plants were flowering alongside the emerged leaves of the next generation. Patience is needed when studying the pollination of Caleana major, as insect visitation is meagre in natural populations and insects are not readily attracted to flowers placed out during baiting studies. A couple of reports showed that the flowers of C. major attracted the attention of male sawflies which become effectively trapped between the triggered labellum and the column. The sawflies were identified as Lophyrotoma leachii (Cady 1965) from observations made at Narooma, N.S.W.; and a species of Pterygophorus (Bates 1989) near Wauchope, N.S.W. Photographs of four species of Lophyrotoma trapped in the flowers and/or carrying pollinia are presented in Kuiter (2016, page 111 and 2017). Identified as L. interrupta, L. nigripes, L. ramosa and L. zonalis, these images clearly show the sawfly on the labellum with its head held close to the beak, or trapped headfirst between the labellum and column. Sexual deception most likely plays a role in the pollination of this species and at least one image in Kuiter 2017 shows a male sawfly standing on the beak of the ducks-head labellum with its abdomen apparently probing the head in a pseudocopulatory posture. Further research is obviously needed to determine the number of sawfly species involved in the pollination of C. major. The flowers of C. major can be very long-lived (6--10 weeks) and successful pollination is rare. Indeed, the pioneering Australian orchid botanist R.D. Fitzgerald records seeing no insect visits and only 4 capsules developing in a population of 127 flowers that he monitored in 1878 near Sydney. By comparison, Caleana minor is much more frequently pollinated and commonly produces capsules. For more details on Caleana major pollination see Bower 2001: 141--143.

Flowering occurs regularly in open habitats, and is enhanced by summer fires in dense habitats. At Mullion Creek, N.S.W., Caleana minor is pollinated by males of a completely black species of thynnine wasp, Thynnoturneria armiger (Bower 2014), whereas in parts of Vic. species of Neozeleboria are actively involved (Kuiter 2016). Further research is needed over the natural range of C. minor to clarify details of its pollination in different regions and habitats and the possible involvement of cryptic species (both in the orchid and the wasps). The males of other species of thynnine wasp may also be attracted to the flowers of C. minor (Bower 1992, 2007; Bower & Brown 2009) because of similar, but not identical, sex pheromones (see Kuiter 2016, 2017; Kuiter & Findlater-Smith 2018). Apomixis is known to occur in C. minor (Clements 1995). All plants in S.A. are apparently totally apomictic, attracting no pollinating insects, the ovaries swelling even before the flowers open and becoming quite swollen and turgid early in anthesis (Bates 1984, Bates & Weber 1990, Bates 2006). By contrast the ovaries of non-apomictic C. minor are not swollen in early flower and the flowers usually attract wasps for pollination. Freak variants of C. minor in the Blue Mountains of N.S.W. and around the Grampians in western Vic. are able to reproduce by apomixis. These freaks, which form small, localised patches in some areas, have abortive labella which cannot function normally and malformed columns and anthers which may or may not contain pollen.

2 apomictic variants have been formally named as distinct species. The first, described by Baron von Mueller as Caleya sullivanii in 1882, was based on specimens collected by D. Sullivan in January of that year from near Mt Zero in the southern Grampians, western Vic. It was transferred to Caleana in 1926 and then placed in Paracaleana in 1972. This freak apomictic variant also occurs nearby at Dadswells Bridge where a study showed that plants of P. sullivanii were interspersed with morphologically distinct and apparently normal plants of Caleana minor (Jones 1977). The same study also revealed the extreme aberrant morphology of P. sullivanii. For example, the labellum laminae ranged from a modified structure with only a slight resemblance to the labellum of C. minor, to flat, petaloid, non-glandular structures with no obvious similarities. Additionally the abortive labellum strap was immobile or capable of only slight movement and often the sepals, petals and column were ornamented haphazardly with labellum calli. The column was reduced in size and of a very different shape to a normal column, and the anther was abortive or completely absent. Difference in these abortive features were also found between individual flowers on a single inflorescence, indicating the high degree of instability in the floral morphology. The second freak to be named at species rank was Caleana nublingii which was described by the Victorian orchid botanist W.H. Nicholls in 1931 based on plants collected by Erwin Nubling in 1930 from Bell in the Blue Mountains of N.S.W. Plants and flowers of both these freak taxa are illustrated by colour plates in Nicholls (1969) - P. sullivanii on Plate 176 and C. nublingii on plate 177.

So strong was the attraction that the wasps appeared within minutes of placing a cut inflorescence in the sunlight. Up to 30 wasps have been captured in a day after being attracted to a solitary inflorescence. Sometimes 3 or 4 wasps converge on a single flower, fighting and scrambling for possession. If the flowers are covered, the wasps are still attracted and land on the cover, seeking the flowers. The approach of insects to the flowers is rapid and direct. They land on the labellum with their head near the column and make copulatory movements with the abdomen. The head contacts the friable pollen, dislodging some onto the stigma and a significant amount sticks on the head for transport to another flower.

Chiloglottis cornuta is the most widely distributed species in the genus. The flowers are self-pollinating. In some areas the flowers open freely and have widely spreading lateral sepals and petals and a protruding labellum, often held nearly horizontally. This variant occasionally crosses with C. valida, presumably when the pollinator mistakenly visits the wrong flower. In other areas the flowers do not open widely, sometimes hardly at all, the segments mostly remain incurved and the labellum remains obliquely erect. The labellum calli are extremely variable in number, size, shape (mounded, flat, linear or ridge-like) and colour (green, reddish or black). Calli are occasionally fused into ridge-like structures.

Widespread and often locally common, extending from the coast in some areas (King Island.) to high in the mountains. Found growing among shrubs, ferns, moss colonies and deep forest litter in shady, humid, sheltered sites in tall, moist to wet forest, including wet sclerophyll forest dominated by mountain ash, rainforest dominated by myrtle beech, streamside vegetation, fern gullies and coastal scrub in freely draining to moisture-retentive loam; plants occasionally grow in shallow running water. It also colonises litter on boulders, rotting logs, living and dead tree fern trunks and sphagnum mounds in subalpine areas. In S.A. it grows in bogs with sphagnum and ferns.

S.A. (Nangwarry in SE), N.S.W. (rare in SE, Snowy Mountains), Vic. (mainly in E & NE, scattered and uncommon in W including the Grampians), Tas. (widespread, King Island, Flinders Island); 50--2000 m altitude; also occurs in New Zealand and Campbell Islands.

The original specimen used to describe Chiloglottis trilabra was a freak peloric flower that had three labella. This species, together with Cryptostylis subulata, Diplodium alatum and Eriochilus cucullatus, was among the earliest Australian orchids to be scientifically described. It was first collected in 1793 by a group of French botanists and biologists, headed by Jacques-Julien Houtou de Labillardière who named the species in 1806 as Epipactis reflexa. These scientists, who were on a French expedition which visited south-eastern Tas. while searching for the lost expedition of La Pérouse, collected around Recherche Bay for five weeks between January and May 1793. The botanical results of the collections, including illustrations, were published in two volumes entitled Nova Hollandiae Plantarum Specimen in 1804--1806. Epipactis reflexa was illustrated on tab. 211 in the second volume. The type specimens and/or original illustrations of Labillardière’s Australian orchids are housed in the Herbarium at the University of Florence in Italy.

Qld (NE: restricted to a small area S of Cooktown); 300--500 m altitude.
